task_title: Logbook Entries Related to Instrument Instruction
objective: By the end of this lesson you can write and explain every entry an instrument instructor signs: instrument training given in the airplane, in a simulator or training device and on the ground; the instrument rating knowledge and practical test endorsements with the 8710 recommendation; the IPC endorsement and what to log when an IPC is not satisfactory; and the records you must keep and for how long. You can also teach a learner to log instrument time and approaches correctly.
why: Your entry is the proof that instrument training happened: a pilot must record the training and experience used for a rating or for currency [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(a)]], and you must sign the logbook of everyone you train in the air or on the ground [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(a)]]. Examiners and inspectors accept your recommendation as evidence that an applicant is qualified [[25:203|AIH C-2]], and the FAA may hold you accountable for an endorsement given to someone who does not meet the rules [[25:184|AIH 9-14]]. FAA-S-8081-9E tells the evaluator to select this Task in Area II, so expect to describe and write these entries on your checkride.

warmup: Think first: a pilot you have never flown with asks for an IPC. His logbook shows his last six approaches 14 months ago, all written as "6 appr, sim" with no places, plus 9 hours of simulator time that nobody signed. Two hours later he has flown well except one sloppy hold, which you retrained and he then flew to standard. What do you write in his logbook, what do you keep for yourself, and what will you teach him about his own entries?

key_terms.def: A ground instructor current under 61.217 or a flight instructor current under 61.197, acting within the privileges of the certificate, or a person the Administrator authorizes [[12:30|AC 61-65K 37]] [[12:31|AC 61-65K 37]].

The instructor's legible endorsement of logged training: a description of the training, the length of the lesson, and the instructor's signature, certificate number and expiration or recent experience end date [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]].
Flight time when the pilot operates the aircraft solely by reference to instruments, in actual or simulated instrument conditions [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(1)]].
Separate conditions of flight in the logbook: actual instrument, or simulated instrument in flight or in a FFS, FTD or ATD [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(b)(3)]].

The end of your 24-calendar-month recent experience period; the AC's examples run a period through the last day of its final month (for example, valid through August 31). It goes in the signature block of a certificate without an expiration date [[12:40|AC 61-65K A-7]] [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(a)]] [[12:27|AC 61-65K 30.3.2]].
The check that restores instrument currency after more than six calendar months out; it includes the areas of operation in the Instrument Rating ACS [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].
The AC 61-65K instrument practical test endorsements: A.43 for the training of 61.65(c) and (d), A.44 for the 61.39(a) prerequisites [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.43]] [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.44]].
The AC 61-65K endorsement for a satisfactory IPC. No logbook entry reflecting unsatisfactory performance on an IPC is required [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.71]].
The three FAA categories of flight simulation trainers. FFSs and FTDs are qualified under part 60; ATDs are approved, as basic (BATD) or advanced (AATD) [[25:172|AIH 9-2]] [[25:173|AIH 9-3]].
The FAA letter for an ATD model that sets the training credit it may give. It is valid for five years, and the pilot in training should keep a copy [[25:173|AIH 9-3]] [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].
A ground instructor rating that allows ground training for the instrument rating and for an IPC, and the recommendation for the instrument knowledge test [[60:354|14 CFR 61.215(c)]].
The test report that lists the applicant's deficient subject areas; A.44 certifies the applicant now has satisfactory knowledge of them [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.44]] [[12:10|AC 61-65K 14]].

chunks.title: Who may give instrument training, and what you may sign

body.p: This lesson covers the instrument instructor's side of the logbook. The Instrument lesson IR.I.A covers the pilot's side (currency, the IPC and logging approaches), and the CFI lesson AI.II.K covers endorsements in general. Here we add what you log and sign as a CFII.

Apart from a few listed exceptions, such as a ground instructor endorsing a logbook for the training he gave [[60:191|14 CFR 61.3(d)(3)(iv)]], only a flight instructor with the appropriate rating on the certificate may endorse an applicant for a pilot certificate or rating, or endorse a logbook to show training given [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(d)(2)]]. Your certificate lets you train and endorse for, among other things, an instrument rating, a recency of experience requirement, a practical test and a knowledge test [[60:345|14 CFR 61.193(a)]].

callout.text: You may not endorse a pilot's logbook for an instrument proficiency check unless you tested that pilot under 61.57(d) yourself [[60:347|14 CFR 61.195(d)(6)]].

body.p: The logging rules sit in several sections that must be read together: 61.189 for your signature and records, 61.193 for what you may endorse, the training rules such as 61.65 for what the learner must log, and 61.51 for what goes in each entry [[25:202|AIH C-1]].

check.q: A CFI without an instrument rating on her instructor certificate offers to give your instrument learner two hours of hood work toward the rating while you are away. What do you tell her?
check.a: She may not. Instrument training for an instrument rating needs an instrument rating on the flight instructor certificate [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(c)]]. A private learner's 3 hours by reference to instruments, by contrast, need not come from a CFII [[12:19|AC 61-65K 23]].

chunks.title: K1: The entry for every instrument lesson

body.p: **Logbook entries or training records for instrument flight/instrument flight instruction or ground instruction given.** You must sign the logbook of each person you give flight or ground training [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(a)]]. A person may log training time received from an authorized instructor in an aircraft, FFS, FTD or ATD [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(h)(1)]]. That time must be in a logbook, endorsed legibly by you, and include [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]]:

bullets: A description of the training given.
The length of the training lesson.
Your signature, certificate number, and certificate expiration date or recent experience end date.

body.p: The learner's line for the same lesson carries the general items: date, total time, where the aircraft departed and arrived (or where a simulator or FTD lesson took place), type and identification of the aircraft or device, and the safety pilot's name if 91.109 requires one [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(b)(1)]]. It shows the kind of training, such as flight and ground training received from an authorized instructor, or device training from one [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(b)(2)(iv)]] [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(b)(2)(v)]]. And it shows the conditions: day or night, actual instrument, or simulated instrument in flight or in a device [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(b)(3)]].

head: Part
What the rule asks
Example (Application)
rows: A description of the training given [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]]
"Partial panel: compass and timed turns, unusual attitude recoveries. VOR holding, direct and teardrop entries."
The length of the training lesson [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]]
Actual instrument, or simulated instrument in flight or in a device [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(b)(3)]]
Signature, date signed, certificate number, RE end date or expiration date; printed name optional [[12:40|AC 61-65K A-7]]

callout.text: Application: describe the lesson in the words of the Task you trained, not just "instrument dual." Training records are the basis for later endorsements and test recommendations [[25:150|AIH 7-6]], so the CFII who signs A.43 will read these lines, and it may be you.

check.q: A new CFII signs a lesson with "Instrument dual, 1.5" and his signature. What is missing under 61.51(h)?
check.a: A description of what was taught, and in the signature block his certificate number and the expiration or RE end date [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]].

chunks.title: K1: In the airplane: actual, simulated, and who logs what

body.p: **Instrument flight instruction given.** Only time when a pilot operates the aircraft solely by reference to instruments, in actual or simulated conditions, is instrument time [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(1)]]. The IFH says the same: log it while you control the aircraft solely by the instruments, with a view-limiting device, in an approved device or in actual IMC [[23:11|IFH viii]].

head: Who
May log
Rule
rows: Rated learner flying under the hood
PIC as sole manipulator of an aircraft for which rated; simulated instrument time; training received
PIC for all the flight time while serving as the authorized instructor, if rated to act as PIC of that aircraft
You, teaching in actual instrument conditions
You, teaching while the learner is under the hood in VMC
No instrument time: you are not flying solely by instruments, and (g)(2) covers only actual conditions

body.p: In cloud, both of you may log the actual time: the learner because she is flying solely by instruments [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(1)]], you because you are giving instrument instruction in actual conditions [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(2)]]. A visual departure or a climb before entering the cloud is not instrument time for either of you [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(1)]].
Watch your own limit: in any 24 consecutive hours you may not conduct more than 8 hours of flight training [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]]. A long IFR cross-country plus an evening lesson can reach it.

callout.text: Under the hood the learner cannot see out. During a check flown under IFR or with a view-limiting device in VMC, AC 61-98E makes it the instructor's responsibility to stay vigilant for other aircraft through all phases of flight [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.3.1]]. Application: treat every hood lesson the same way.

check.q: A 2.0-hour lesson: 0.3 visual climb-out, 1.2 in cloud, 0.5 under the hood after breaking out. What instrument time do you log, and what does the learner log?
check.a: You log 1.2 actual, the time instructing in actual conditions [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(2)]]. The learner logs 1.2 actual and 0.5 simulated, the time flown solely by instruments [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(1)]]. The 0.3 visual climb is instrument time for neither of you.

chunks.title: K1: Simulator, FTD and ATD lessons

body.p: Instrument time in a FFS, FTD or ATD counts toward a certificate or rating only if an authorized instructor is present to observe it and signs the logbook or training record to verify the time and the content of the session [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(4)]]. For currency, the pilot needs only a logbook or training record that names the device, the time and the content [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(5)]].

bullets: FFS or FTD: log and record the FAA ID number or serial number of the device. These devices are requalified every year, so check that the qualification is current [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].
ATD: log the time as BATD or AATD time and record the manufacturer and model. LOAs are valid for five years, and the pilot in training should keep a copy [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].
The LOA for each ATD model says which training credit or experience it can give [[25:173|AIH 9-3]]. For currency, an ATD counts as its LOA specifies [[15:21|AC 61-98E 3.2]].

head: Device time toward the instrument-airplane rating
Maximum credit
rows: FFS or FTD, time given by an authorized instructor, not under part 142
FFS or FTD under a part 142 program
BATD, when the device, the training and the tasks are FAA-approved and an authorized instructor gives the time
All devices together, except the part 142 case

body.p: There is no limit on how much device time can be logged; part 61 limits how much can be credited toward a certificate or rating [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. So keep the columns honest and let the 61.65 caps decide what counts.

callout.text: An ATD may not be used for a practical test for a certificate or rating [[12:9|AC 61-65K 12.4]] [[25:173|AIH 9-3]].

check.q: Your learner has 14 hours in an AATD and 9 in an FTD, all with an instructor and not under part 142. How much device time can count toward the 40 hours?
check.a: 20 hours. Each device type alone would be under its cap, but all devices together are limited to 20 hours outside part 142 [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(i)]] [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(j)]].

chunks.title: K1: Ground instruction given and the knowledge test endorsement

body.p: **Ground instruction given.** An instrument rating applicant must receive and log ground training from an authorized instructor, or complete a home-study course, on the 61.65(b) knowledge areas [[60:250|14 CFR 61.65(a)(3)]]. They run from the IFR regulations and the AIM through ATC, navigation and approaches, IFR charts, weather and windshear, to ADM and crew resource management [[60:250|14 CFR 61.65(b)]].

You sign for ground training just as for flight training [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(a)]], and the learner logs it as ground training received from an authorized instructor [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(b)(2)(iv)]]. Give it the same description and length as a flight lesson.

The knowledge test needs a logbook or training record endorsement that the applicant is prepared [[60:250|14 CFR 61.65(a)(4)]]. AC 61-65K A.42 reads: "I certify that [First name, MI, Last name] has received the required training of 14 CFR § 61.65(b). I have determined that they are prepared for the Instrument–[airplane, helicopter, or powered-lift] knowledge test." [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.42]]

bullets: Home study: an applicant may bring an individually developed home-study course to a flight or ground instructor, who reviews it, questions the applicant and then endorses that the applicant is prepared [[12:7|AC 61-65K 10.2]].

An instrument ground instructor may give this ground training and the ground training for an IPC, recommend for the instrument knowledge test, and endorse the logbook for that training [[60:354|14 CFR 61.215(c)]] [[60:354|14 CFR 61.215(d)]].

Failed knowledge test: the applicant needs an endorsement from an authorized instructor who gave additional training; the knowledge test report has an unsigned endorsement you may use [[25:204|AIH C-3]] [[60:227|14 CFR 61.49(a)(2)]].
A pilot who already holds an instrument rating, such as instrument-helicopter, takes no new knowledge test [[60:250|14 CFR 61.65(a)(7)]].

callout.text: Application: list the ten 61.65(b) areas in your ground syllabus with a box beside each. When endorsements and recordkeeping are designed into the syllabus, training is easier to track and records easier to certify [[25:129|AIH 5-26]].

check.q: Your learner did all her instrument ground training with an instrument ground instructor. Who may sign her knowledge test endorsement?
check.a: The ground instructor may: an IGI may recommend for the instrument knowledge test and endorse the logbook for that training [[60:354|14 CFR 61.215(c)]] [[60:354|14 CFR 61.215(d)]]. You may as well, once you are satisfied she is prepared [[60:345|14 CFR 61.193(a)]].

chunks.title: Teaching your learner to log instrument time and approaches

body.p: Learners copy what they see in your entries, and the time they use for a rating or for currency must be documented [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(a)]]. Teach the logbook in the first instrument lesson and check it at every lesson after.

head: Teach this
Why
Rule
rows: Log instrument time only while flying solely by instruments
Takeoff and the climb before the hood goes on, or before the cloud, are not instrument time
They are separate conditions of flight
For each approach used for currency, write its location and type
Write the safety pilot's name when one is required
A general entry item and a currency item
Log holding and intercepting and tracking, not only approaches
Device lessons: device ID or serial (ATD maker and model), time and content
Needed for currency credit and to verify rating credit

body.p: AC 61-98E Appendix G is a sample instrument experience summary: total and recent time, IMC, night IFR, approaches, approaches to minimums and approaches in the last 6 months [[15:44|AC 61-98E G-1]]. Have the learner fill one in from the logbook before the checkride. If the totals are hard to find, the entries need work.

Teach it with the demonstration-performance method: explain the rule, fill in one lesson line yourself while saying each part aloud, have the learner log the next lesson while you coach, then check one he does alone [[25:124|AIH 5-21]] [[25:125|AIH 5-22]].

callout.text: Every instrument line: actual or sim, how long, each approach with type and place, holding and tracking, the safety pilot's name, and on dual lessons the instructor's signature with certificate number and RE date.

check.q: Your learner flew an RNAV approach and an ILS under the hood with a friend as safety pilot and logged "2 approaches, 1.3 sim." What must he add for the approaches to count toward 61.57(c)?
check.a: The location and type of each approach and the safety pilot's name [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)]].

chunks.title: K2: Audit the logbook before you recommend

body.p: **Preparation of a recommendation for an instrument rating practical test, including appropriate logbook entry,** starts with the logbook. The IFH puts it on you: the recommending instructor must make sure the applicant meets the 14 CFR part 61 requirements and is prepared, including training, knowledge, experience and the instructor endorsements [[23:344|IFH B-3]].

head: Check
Requirement
Rule
rows: 50 hours, at least 10 in airplanes; a combined private and instrument applicant may credit up to 45 hours of PIC-duty cross-country with an instructor
40 hours, actual or simulated, in the 61.65(c) areas of operation
15 of the 40 hours from an authorized instructor with an instrument-airplane rating
3 hours of instrument flight training in an airplane within 2 calendar months before the date of the practical test
With an instructor, under IFR on a filed flight plan; 250 NM along airways or ATC routing; an approach at each airport; three different kinds of approaches
20 hours total in devices (30 under part 142); BATD 10, AATD 20
Logged training on all eight 61.65(c) areas, from preflight preparation to postflight procedures
Ground training or home study logged; knowledge test passed within the 24 calendar months before the month the practical test is completed

body.p: Count only proper entries. Device time toward the rating needs the signature of the instructor who was present to observe it [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(4)]], and training time needs the instructor's endorsement with a description and length [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]]. Because the rule asks for the observing instructor's signature, you cannot sign device time you did not watch.

callout.text: Application: keep a one-page audit sheet with these rows and the logbook page for each, and file it in the learner's training folder. The AIH recommends a folder that holds training requirements, instruction received and the part 61 requirements met [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

check.q: Your applicant's checkride is November 18, 2026. He passed the knowledge test in October 2024. Can he test?
check.a: No. The knowledge test must be passed within the 24 calendar months before the month he completes the practical test, here November 2024 through October 2026 [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(1)]]. October 2024 is outside that window, so he must pass it again first.

chunks.title: K2: The practical test endorsements and the 8710 recommendation

body.p: **Including appropriate logbook entry.** 61.65(a)(6) requires a logbook or training record endorsement that the applicant is prepared for the practical test [[60:250|14 CFR 61.65(a)(6)]]. 61.39 requires an endorsement that the applicant received and logged training within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application, is prepared, and has shown satisfactory knowledge of the areas missed on the knowledge test [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)]]. AC 61-65K has two instrument endorsements for this:

head: Endorsement
AC 61-65K wording
rows: "I certify that [First name, MI, Last name] has received the required training of 14 CFR § 61.65(c) and (d). I have determined they are prepared for the Instrument–[airplane, helicopter, or powered-lift] practical test." [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.43]]
A.44 Prerequisites for instrument practical tests: 14 CFR § 61.39(a)

"I certify that [First name, MI, Last name] has received and logged the required flight time/training of 14 CFR § 61.39(a) in preparation for the practical test within 2 calendar months preceding the date of the test and has satisfactory knowledge of the subject areas in which they were shown to be deficient by the FAA Airman Knowledge Test Report. I have determined they are prepared for the Instrument–[airplane, helicopter, or powered-lift] practical test." [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.44]]

body.p: The wording need not match the AC exactly, though the AIH recommends wording endorsements as closely as possible to AC 61-65, and at a minimum you must cite the 14 CFR part 61 section completed [[25:183|AIH 9-13]] [[25:202|AIH C-1]]. Each endorsement still needs your signature, the date, your certificate number and your RE end date [[12:40|AC 61-65K A-7]].

The recommendation: the application form has a block for your written recommendation, and signing it is a serious responsibility. Have the applicant demonstrate the knowledge and skill for the rating first, never less than the complete procedure in the ACS or PTS [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. Use IACRA when possible; it checks entries, while a mistake on a paper form can delay the certificate [[25:203|AIH C-2]].

bullets: The test may be in an airplane, or in a FFS or FTD appropriate to the rating; in an FTD the approaches are limited to one precision and one nonprecision [[60:250|14 CFR 61.65(a)(8)]]. An ATD may not be used [[12:9|AC 61-65K 12.4]].

Retest after a Notice of Disapproval: a new endorsement that the applicant received the training and is prepared, and your recommendation on the 8710 for each retest [[12:11|AC 61-65K 14.2]] [[60:227|14 CFR 61.49(a)(2)]].
Letter of Discontinuance: no new endorsement; credit for areas passed lasts 60 calendar days [[12:11|AC 61-65K 14.3]].
Record the endorsement in your own records, with the kind of test, the date and the result [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(b)(2)]].

callout.text: Make the dates fit both rules. 61.65(d)(2)(i) counts 2 calendar months before the date of the test; 61.39(a)(6)(i) counts 2 calendar months before the month of application [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(i)]] [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)(i)]]. Application: fly the last 3 airplane hours and sign A.43 and A.44 close to the test.

check.q: Which two AC 61-65K endorsements do you write for an instrument-airplane practical test, and what does the second add?
check.a: A.43 under 61.65(a)(6) and A.44 under 61.39(a). A.44 certifies training within 2 calendar months and satisfactory knowledge of the areas missed on the knowledge test [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.43]] [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.44]].

chunks.title: K3: Who may give an IPC and how to run it

body.p: A pilot who has missed the 61.57(c) instrument experience for more than six calendar months can restore currency only with an IPC [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]]. The Instrument lesson IR.I.A covers the pilot's side; this is the instructor's.

head: Item
What the sources say
rows: An examiner, an authorized instructor, certain military and company check pilots, or a person approved by the Administrator [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(3)]]. An instructor needs an instrument rating on both the pilot and the instructor certificate for the category and class used [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]].
You should also meet the currency requirements for your pilot and instructor certificates, and consider your own instrument currency [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]].

The Instrument Rating ACS areas of operation for the rating held [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]], including the tasks in its Rating Task Table, plus any maneuver you need to see [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.3]].

An aircraft of the category, or a FFS or FTD that represents it [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(2)]]. AC 61-98E adds that all or part of it, as the instrument ACS or PTS specifies, may be done in an approved device: an FFS or FTD needs an FAA-approved IPC checking program (61.4), and among ATDs only an AATD may be used, within its LOA [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.2]].
Part 91, charts and procedures, weather, preflight planning, IFR systems and instruments, IFR airworthiness, ATC procedures and angle of attack [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.2.1]] [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.2.1]].

To fully evaluate the pilot, you may have him fly a short IFR cross-country with at least part of it in the system [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.2.2]]; always sound basic attitude instrument flying, and a view-limiting device when not in actual conditions [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.3]].

body.p: Structure it like a flight review: agree on the conditions, use the Appendix G summary to shape the ground review, build a scenario plan of action, and agree on how the check will run and what counts as satisfactory before you start [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.3.1]] [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.3.2]] [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.3.3]] [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.4]]. The Appendix I checklist runs in five steps: preparation, ground review, flight activities, postflight discussion, and an aeronautical health maintenance and improvement plan [[15:46|AC 61-98E I-1]].

callout.text: An instrument ground instructor may give the ground training for an IPC [[60:354|14 CFR 61.215(c)]], but as a flight instructor you may sign the IPC only after you have tested the pilot under 61.57(d) yourself [[60:347|14 CFR 61.195(d)(6)]].

check.q: A pilot asks for an IPC in your school's BATD to save money. What do you say?
check.a: Not in a BATD. AC 61-98E allows only an AATD, within its LOA [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.2]], and the rule itself names an aircraft, FFS or FTD [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(2)]].

chunks.title: K3: The IPC endorsement, and when you do not sign

body.p: **Required endorsement of a pilot logbook for satisfactory completion of an instrument proficiency check.** AC 61-98E says to make it in accordance with AC 61-65 [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.2]]. AC 61-65K A.71 reads: "I certify that [First name, MI, Last name], [grade of pilot certificate], [certificate number], has satisfactorily completed the instrument proficiency check of 14 CFR § 61.57(d) in a [M/M] aircraft on [date]." [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.71]]

head: Outcome
What you write and do
rows: A.71 with your signature block [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.71]] [[12:40|AC 61-65K A-7]]. The pilot also logs the flight, since experience used for recent flight experience must be recorded [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(a)(2)]].

No logbook entry reflecting unsatisfactory performance is required [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.71]]. Do not endorse an unsatisfactory IPC; log the session as "dual instruction given" [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.1]].
Pilot does not meet the FAA English language standard
Do not endorse it as complete. Log the training received, advise the pilot and contact the responsible FSDO [[12:8|AC 61-65K 11.4.2]].
Give a comprehensive analysis of the performance with suggestions for the weak areas [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.4]] [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4]].

bullets: An 8710-1 for an IPC is optional, though the FAA strongly encourages it; IACRA is the preferred method [[15:8|AC 61-98E 1.10.2]] [[15:8|AC 61-98E 1.10.3]].
You may keep the IPC plan of action for an appropriate period as a record of its scope and content; 61.189 does not require it [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.2]].

You may combine a flight review with the 61.57 requirements [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(h)]]. The proficiency checks that replace a flight review are those conducted by an examiner, an approved pilot check airman or a U.S. Armed Force [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(d)(1)]], so if you also gave a flight review, endorse it too (A.69) [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.69]].

callout.text: Satisfactory IPC: A.71 with grade, certificate number, M/M and date. Not satisfactory: "dual instruction given," never a failure entry.

check.q: Your IPC candidate flies everything well except the approaches, which stay outside standards after retraining. What goes in her logbook?
check.a: A "dual instruction given" entry for the training, not an unsatisfactory IPC entry [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.1]] [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.71]], and a debrief with a plan for the weak areas [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4]].

body.p: **Required flight instructor records.** 14 CFR 61.189 has three parts [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189]]:

head: Rule
What you must do
Instrument example
rows: Sign the logbook of each person you give flight or ground training [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(a)]]
Every hood, actual, device and ground lesson you give
Keep the name of each person you endorsed for solo flight privileges, and the date [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(b)(1)]]
Rare for a CFII, but required whenever you sign one
Keep the name of each person you endorsed for a knowledge or practical test, with the kind of test, the date and the results [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(b)(2)]]
Your A.42, A.43 and A.44 endorsements
Keep these records at least 3 years [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(c)]]
An A.43 signed in March 2026 stays on file until at least March 2029

body.p: The record may be a logbook or a separate document [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(b)]]. The AIH describes it as the type of endorsement, the name and the date, with the kind of test, date and results for test endorsements [[25:203|AIH C-2]].

bullets: Training folder: lesson plans, training requirements, flight or ground instruction received, part 61 requirements met and solo endorsements, kept at least 3 years; many records are now electronic [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].
IPC plan of action: not required by 61.189, but you may keep it as a record of the IPC's scope and content [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.2]].

Your pass record pays off. Endorsing at least 5 applicants in 24 calendar months with at least 80 percent passing the first time is one way to keep recent experience, if you submit documentation of it [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(b)(2)(i)]]. For a Gold Seal certificate you need, among other things, a ground instructor certificate with an advanced or instrument rating and, within the previous 24 calendar months, at least 10 applicants trained and recommended with at least 80 percent passing on the first attempt; 20 practical tests as an examiner or part 141 chief instructor, or a mix of the two, also qualify [[12:24|AC 61-65K 28]].

check.q: An examiner asks what your 61.189 record shows for an instrument applicant you endorsed. What do you list?
check.a: The applicant's name, the kind of test (instrument-airplane practical test), the date and the result, kept at least 3 years [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189]].

chunks.title: K4: Your own logbook, limits and currency

body.p: Your records also protect you. Keep your own logbook as carefully as your learner's.

bullets: PIC time: you may log all flight time while serving as the authorized instructor, if rated to act as PIC of that aircraft [[60:229|14 CFR 61.51(e)(3)]].
Instrument time: only when giving instrument instruction in actual instrument conditions [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(2)]].

RE end date: it goes in every training entry and endorsement you sign [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)(ii)]] [[12:40|AC 61-65K A-7]], and you may instruct only within your 24-calendar-month recent experience period [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(a)]].
Carry your flight instructor certificate, or other documentation acceptable to the Administrator, when you instruct [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(d)(1)]].
Be qualified in each role and each make and model. If you are not proficient in an aircraft or role, decline and help the pilot find a qualified instructor [[15:19|AC 61-98E 2.4.1]].

body.p: If you are PIC on an IFR training flight, you need your own instrument currency [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]]. Before an IPC, AC 61-98E asks you to consider your own instrument currency as well [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]].

callout.text: Your signature is only as good as your RE date. If your recent experience period ends, you may not exercise instructor privileges until they are reinstated [[60:352|14 CFR 61.197(c)]], so no lessons, no endorsements and no IPCs.

check.q: You fly a 2.5-hour IFR training flight as the authorized instructor, 1.0 of it in cloud, with your rated learner flying. What do you log?
check.a: 2.5 PIC as the authorized instructor, if you are rated for that aircraft [[60:229|14 CFR 61.51(e)(3)]], and 1.0 actual instrument [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(2)]].

chunks.title: How to teach it and how the examiner tests it

body.p: FAA-S-8081-9E has the evaluator select Task D in Area II, and it lists knowledge of the instructor's responsibilities for logbook entries and endorsements among the measures of satisfactory performance. Expect to describe entries and to write them.

head: Element
What the examiner may ask
Start your answer with
rows: Write today's entry for a hood lesson and for an AATD lesson
The 61.51(h)(2) items and conditions; for the device, your observed-and-signed statement [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]] [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(4)]]
Is this applicant eligible? Write the endorsements
Write an IPC endorsement. What if it is not satisfactory?
Which records do you keep, and how long?
Names, kind of test, date and results, for at least 3 years [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189]]

body.p: Teaching entries to a learner or a new instructor is a mental skill, so the demonstration-performance method fits: explain the rule, demonstrate one entry aloud, let the learner write one with coaching, then have them write one alone while you evaluate [[25:124|AIH 5-21]] [[25:125|AIH 5-22]].

After an IPC or a mock checkride, debrief with the collaborative critique: replay, reconstruct, reflect and redirect [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]. Step 4 of the Appendix I IPC checklist uses the same four ideas [[15:46|AC 61-98E I-1]].

callout.text: Application: bring blank logbook pages and AC 61-65K Appendix A to the checkride. Write A.42, A.43, A.44 and A.71 from memory, then check them against the AC.

check.q: In the demonstration-performance method, what happens in the evaluation phase when you teach a new CFII to write A.71?
check.a: The learner works alone, and you judge how well the skill was mastered compared with how it was taught [[25:125|AIH 5-22]].

body.p: These are the errors you will find when you take over a learner, give an IPC, or audit your own logbook.

head: Error
What you see
Fix
rows: Description, lesson length, certificate number and RE date [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]]
Unsigned device time counted toward the rating
AATD hours with no instructor signature
Only time an instructor observed and signed counts [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(4)]]
FFS or FTD ID or serial; ATD maker and model, as BATD or AATD [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]
Location and type of each, and the safety pilot's name [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)]]
Instructor logs hood time as instrument time
Last airplane instrument training four months before the test
3 hours in an airplane within 2 calendar months before the test [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(i)]]
No aircraft make and model or date
Name, kind of test, date, result, kept at least 3 years [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(b)(2)]] [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(c)]]

callout.text: A self-endorsement is never valid: you may not endorse yourself for a certificate, rating, flight review, authorization, operating privilege, practical test or knowledge test [[60:349|14 CFR 61.195(i)]].

check.q: A learner shows 26 hours in an AATD with an instructor and 16 in the airplane. Does she have the 40 hours of instrument time?
check.a: No. Only 20 device hours count outside part 142 [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(j)]], so she has 36 creditable hours and needs 4 more in the airplane.

scenario.title: Inheriting an instrument learner before the checkride
scenario.setup: You join a flight school in October 2026. Dana, a private pilot ASEL, is booked for her instrument-airplane practical test on November 18, 2026. Her previous CFII has left the school. Her logbook shows 24.0 hours of actual and simulated instrument time in the airplane (13.0 with the previous CFII, 11.0 with you this month); 12.0 hours in the school's AATD, 8.0 signed by the previous CFII and 4.0 marked "practice, solo"; a cross-country under an IFR flight plan with the previous CFII logged only as "IFR XC 255 NM, 3 approaches"; 62 hours of cross-country PIC; and a knowledge test passed in October 2024.

questions.q: How much of her instrument time can you count toward the 40 hours today?
questions.a: 32.0 hours: the 24.0 in the airplane plus the 8.0 AATD hours an instructor observed and signed [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(4)]], well under the 20-hour AATD cap [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(i)]]. The 4.0 solo AATD hours do not count toward the rating; with a record of device, time and content they can count for currency [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(5)]]. She needs 8 more hours.

questions.q: Does the cross-country entry show that 61.65(d)(2)(ii) is met?
questions.a: Not yet. The rule needs an instructor, IFR on a filed flight plan, 250 NM along airways or ATC routing, an approach at each airport and three different kinds of approaches [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(ii)]]. "3 approaches" does not show the kinds or the airports. The entry is the training endorsement of the instructor who gave it [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]], so ask the previous CFII to complete the description, or fly the cross-country again with her.

It will have expired. For a November 2026 test it must have been passed in the 24 calendar months before that month, November 2024 through October 2026 [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(1)]]. She must pass it again first, with a knowledge test endorsement such as A.42 [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.42]].

questions.q: Assume she fixes everything and flies to standard. What do you write before the checkride?
questions.a: A.43 under 61.65(a)(6) and A.44 under 61.39(a), each with your signature, date, certificate number and RE end date [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.43]] [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.44]] [[12:40|AC 61-65K A-7]], plus your recommendation on her application, preferably in IACRA [[25:203|AIH C-2]]. Check that she has 3 hours of airplane instrument training within 2 calendar months before the test date [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(i)]].

questions.q: She passes. What goes into your records, and for how long?
questions.a: Her name, the kind of test, the date and the result, kept at least 3 years [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189]]. It also counts toward your first-time pass rate, one way to keep recent experience [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(b)(2)(i)]].

questions.q: In the debrief she asks how to log approaches when she flies with a safety pilot. What do you teach?
questions.a: Log only the time flown solely by instruments [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(1)]]; for each approach, the location and type, and the safety pilot's name [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)]]; and log holding and intercepting and tracking too, since all three are currency tasks [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].

skills.do: Given a sample logbook, audit it aloud against 61.65(d) and 61.39(a), then write A.43 and A.44 with a full signature block and explain each part as you would to a new instructor.
skills.practice: Have another applicant plant three errors in a logbook copy (unsigned device time, a stale knowledge test, a cross-country without approach types) and find them [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)]] [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(4)]] [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(1)]].

skills.do: Write an A.71 IPC endorsement and the "dual instruction given" entry for an IPC that was not satisfactory, and explain why there is no failure entry.
skills.practice: Run a mock IPC debrief with the Appendix I checklist, write both entries from memory, then check them against A.71 and AC 61-98E 5.4.1 [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.71]] [[15:46|AC 61-98E I-1]] [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.1]].

quiz.q: A commercial applicant asks you, a CFI with no instrument rating on your instructor certificate, to give the 10 hours of instrument training 61.129 requires. What applies?
options: Yes, since a commercial certificate is not an instrument rating
Yes, if your pilot certificate holds an instrument rating
No; it needs an instrument rating on your CFI certificate
Yes, if a CFII countersigns each of the entries afterward
quiz.why: 61.195(c) requires an instrument rating on the flight instructor certificate for the instrument training required for the commercial certificate [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(c)]] [[60:314|14 CFR 61.129(a)(3)(i)]]. An instrument rating on the pilot certificate alone does not meet it.

quiz.q: You and your learner fly 1.6 hours: 0.4 visual departure, 0.9 in cloud, then 0.3 under the hood after breaking out. How much instrument time do you log?
options: 1.6 hours
1.2 hours
None; instructors log only PIC
0.9 hours
quiz.why: An instructor logs instrument time only when giving instruction in actual conditions [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(2)]]. The hood time is the learner's, not yours, because you are not flying solely by instruments [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(1)]].

quiz.q: Your learner flew 2.0 hours in your school's AATD while you watched. What makes it count toward the instrument rating?
options: You observed it and sign the logbook or training record
He records the device, the time and the session content
He flies at least six approaches during the session
The session is flown in an approved part 142 course
quiz.why: Device time counts toward a rating only if an authorized instructor is present to observe it and signs the logbook or training record [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(4)]]. A record of device, time and content is the currency rule, not the rating rule [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(5)]].

quiz.q: What must your learner's logbook show so the approaches she flew with a safety pilot count toward 61.57(c)?
options: The number of approaches and the total simulated time
The location and type of each, and the safety pilot's name
The minimums used and the weather at each airport
An instructor endorsement saying each was flown to the ACS standard
quiz.why: For instrument recency, the logbook must show the location and type of each approach and the safety pilot's name if one was required [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)]].

quiz.q: Your applicant's practical test is on June 20. Which recent training does 61.65(d)(2)(i) require?
options: 3 hours of device training within 60 days of the test
The 250 NM IFR cross-country within 2 calendar months
Six approaches, holding and tracking in the last 6 calendar months
3 hours in an airplane within 2 calendar months of the test
quiz.why: 61.65(d)(2)(i) requires 3 hours of instrument flight training from an authorized instructor in an airplane within 2 calendar months before the date of the practical test [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(i)]]. Six approaches and holding is the 61.57(c) currency rule [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].

quiz.q: An instrument applicant's knowledge test report lists three deficient areas. Which AC 61-65K instrument endorsement certifies that you covered them?
quiz.why: A.44 certifies training within 2 calendar months and satisfactory knowledge of the areas shown deficient on the Airman Knowledge Test Report [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.44]]. A.42 is the knowledge test endorsement and A.43 the 61.65(a)(6) practical test endorsement [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.42]].

quiz.q: A pilot's IPC ends with the holding still below standard after retraining. What goes in his logbook?
options: An entry showing an unsatisfactory IPC and the failed areas
The session logged as dual instruction given, no failure
Nothing at all until he returns and finishes the check
A.71 with a note limiting him to approaches without holds
quiz.why: The instructor should not endorse an unsatisfactory IPC; log the session as "dual instruction given" [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.1]]. No entry reflecting unsatisfactory performance is required [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.71]].

quiz.q: Another CFII flew an IPC with your regular pilot and asks you to sign A.71 for her, since she is leaving town. What applies?
options: You may not; you must have tested the pilot yourself
You may, if she gives you her written notes on the flight
You may, if the pilot also signs a statement that he passed
You may, because you are the pilot's regular instructor
quiz.why: A flight instructor may not endorse a logbook for an IPC unless that instructor tested the pilot under 61.57(d) [[60:347|14 CFR 61.195(d)(6)]].

quiz.q: How long must you keep the record of each instrument practical test endorsement you give?
options: At least 1 year
At least 2 years
At least 5 years
At least 3 years
quiz.why: Records required by 61.189 must be kept at least 3 years [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(c)]].

quiz.q: What must your 61.189 record of a practical test endorsement show?
options: The applicant's total time, instrument time and cross-country time
A copy of the 8710 and of the knowledge test report
The applicant's name, kind of test, the date and the result
The examiner's name and the areas of operation tested
quiz.why: For each person endorsed for a knowledge or practical test: name, kind of test, date and results [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(b)]].

quiz.q: During an IPC flown under the hood in VMC, who must keep watch for other aircraft?
options: The pilot under review, as PIC
You, the instructor, through every phase
ATC, since the flight is on an IFR flight plan
Whoever filed the flight plan for the check
quiz.why: If the check is under IFR, or under VFR with a view-limiting device, it is the instructor's responsibility to remain vigilant for other aircraft throughout all phases of flight [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.3.1]].

quiz.q: Your learner asks why you write "RE 12-31-2027" after your certificate number. What do you tell him?
options: It is your recent experience end date, required with the signature
It is the date your medical certificate expires for flight instructing
It is the date his training record must be reviewed again
It is the date your instrument rating needs its next check
quiz.why: Training entries must include the instructor's certificate expiration date or recent experience end date [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)(ii)]], and AC 61-65K shows the RE format for certificates without an expiration date [[12:40|AC 61-65K A-7]].

final_quiz.q: An instrument ground instructor taught your learner all the 61.65(b) knowledge areas. Who may endorse her for the instrument knowledge test?
options: Only a CFII, because a ground instructor cannot sign
The IGI, who may recommend and endorse for that test
Only the proctor at the knowledge testing center
No one; a course graduation certificate is required
final_quiz.why: An instrument ground instructor may give the instrument rating ground training, recommend for the instrument knowledge test and endorse the logbook for it [[60:354|14 CFR 61.215(c)]] [[60:354|14 CFR 61.215(d)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner logged 18 hours in a BATD with you, 4 in an FTD and 21 in the airplane, none under part 142. How many hours count toward the 40?
final_quiz.why: BATD credit is capped at 10 hours [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(i)]]; with the 4 FTD hours the devices total 14, under the 20-hour cap [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(j)]]. 10 + 4 + 21 = 35.

final_quiz.q: Your applicant passed the instrument knowledge test in May 2025. What is the last month in which she can complete the practical test without retaking it?
options: April 2027
June 2027
May 2027
December 2027
final_quiz.why: The knowledge test must be passed within the 24 calendar months before the month the practical test is completed [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(1)]]. For May 2027 the window is May 2025 through April 2027, which includes May 2025; for June 2027 it does not.

final_quiz.q: Your applicant fails the instrument practical test. What does she need for the retest?
options: A new endorsement and your recommendation on the 8710
Nothing new, if she retests within 60 calendar days
Only a new Airman Knowledge Test Report from her test
A Letter of Discontinuance signed by the examiner
final_quiz.why: After a Notice of Disapproval she needs another endorsement that she received the training and is prepared, and an instructor recommendation on the 8710 for each retest [[12:11|AC 61-65K 14.2]] [[60:227|14 CFR 61.49(a)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: Weather stopped her checkride halfway and the examiner issued a Letter of Discontinuance. What new endorsement does she need to continue?
options: A new A.43 and A.44
A new 8710 recommendation
None is required
A new A.42
final_quiz.why: No additional endorsements are required to continue after a Letter of Discontinuance; credit for areas passed lasts 60 calendar days [[12:11|AC 61-65K 14.3]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot asks for his IPC in your school's FTD. Under the rule and AC 61-98E, is that allowed?
options: No; an IPC must be flown in an aircraft of the category
Only the ground portion may be done in the FTD
No; of all the devices, only an AATD may be used
Yes, if it represents the category and the program is approved
final_quiz.why: An IPC may be given in a FFS or FTD that represents the aircraft category [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(2)]]. If it is done in an FFS or FTD qualified under part 60, the IPC checking program must be approved under 61.4 [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.2]].

final_quiz.q: Look at the sample IPC endorsement. Besides the pilot's name, certificate grade and number, what does it name?
options: The make and model of aircraft and the date
The approaches flown and the airports used
The time logged since the last IPC was given
The ACS tasks the pilot found most difficult
final_quiz.why: A.71 certifies completion of the 61.57(d) IPC "in a [M/M] aircraft on [date]" [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.71]] [[15:46|AC 61-98E I-1]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot asks for an IPC in your school's twin. Your flight instructor certificate has airplane single-engine and instrument-airplane ratings but no multiengine rating; your commercial certificate has AMEL. What applies?
options: You may, since the AMEL rating is on your pilot certificate
You may not; you need both ratings on both certificates
You may, because an IPC is a check and not flight training
You may, if a multiengine CFI rides along in the back
final_quiz.why: An IPC in a multiengine airplane requires an instructor with multiengine and instrument ratings on both the pilot and flight instructor certificates [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]]. The rule sets the same bar for instrument training in a multiengine airplane [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(c)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: During a 3.0-hour IFR lesson you are the authorized instructor and rated in the airplane. How much PIC time may you log?
options: Only the time in actual conditions
Only the time the learner is under the hood
All 3.0 hours
None; the learner is PIC
final_quiz.why: A flight instructor may log PIC for all flight time while serving as the authorized instructor, if rated to act as PIC of that aircraft [[60:229|14 CFR 61.51(e)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot wants you to sign 6 hours of AATD time he flew alone so it counts toward his instrument rating. What do you tell him?
options: You can sign it once he shows you the device's printout
It counts for the rating if he logs device, time and content
It counts if a safety pilot sat in the device with him
Not for the rating; it can count for currency if recorded
final_quiz.why: Device time counts toward a rating only when an authorized instructor was present to observe it and signs [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(4)]]. For currency, a record of device, time and content is enough [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(5)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's long cross-country covered 260 NM with ILS, RNAV and VOR approaches at three airports, flown VFR with a view-limiting device. Does it meet 61.65(d)(2)(ii)?
options: Yes; the distance and the approaches are what count
No; it must be flown under IFR on a filed flight plan
Yes, if the safety pilot's name is in the logbook
No; the flight must cover at least 300 NM in total
final_quiz.why: The cross-country must be performed under instrument flight rules with a flight plan filed with ATC, 250 NM along airways or ATC routing, an approach at each airport and three different kinds of approaches [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(ii)]].

final_quiz.q: Before you sign a practical test recommendation, what demonstration does the AIH say to require?
options: No less than the complete procedure in the ACS or PTS
The three tasks you judge to be the weakest ones
A mock oral only, since the examiner tests the flying
Only the tasks not flown within the past 60 calendar days
final_quiz.why: The applicant should thoroughly demonstrate the required knowledge and skill, in no instance less than the complete procedure in the applicable ACS or PTS [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

final_quiz.q: Your recent experience period ended October 31 and you have not reinstated. On November 10 a pilot asks for an IPC. What applies?
options: You may give it during a 30-day grace period
You may give it, but someone else must sign it
You may give it if an examiner countersigns
You may not use instructor privileges yet
final_quiz.why: A flight instructor who fails to establish recent experience during the 24-calendar-month period may not exercise instructor privileges until they are reinstated under 61.199 [[60:352|14 CFR 61.197(c)]].

final_quiz.q: Why does AC 61-98E suggest keeping the IPC plan of action?
options: 61.189 requires it to be kept for 3 years
The FSDO must receive a copy of each one
As a record of the IPC's scope and content
The pilot must show it at the next IPC
final_quiz.why: Although not required by 61.189, the instructor may keep the plan of action for an appropriate period as a record of the scope and content of the IPC [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.2]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot needs both a flight review and an IPC. What may you do?
options: Combine them at your discretion and endorse each one
Give only the IPC, since it always replaces a review
Give them on separate days at least a week apart
Give only the flight review, since it covers the IPC
final_quiz.why: The flight review may be done together with the 61.57 requirements at the instructor's discretion [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(h)]]. An IPC from an instructor is not among the checks in 61.56(d)(1), so endorse both: A.69 and A.71 [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(d)(1)]] [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.69]].

takeaways: Sign every instrument lesson, in the air, in a device or on the ground: description, length, certificate number and RE date.
Instrument time is only time flown solely by instruments; as the instructor you log it only in actual conditions.
Device time counts toward the rating only if an instructor observed it and signed; then apply the 61.65 device caps.
Teach learners to log each approach with its type and place, holding, tracking and the safety pilot's name.
Before A.43 and A.44, audit 61.65(d), the 3 recent airplane hours, the long IFR cross-country and the knowledge test date.
Satisfactory IPC: A.71 with M/M and date. Not satisfactory: "dual instruction given," never a failure entry.
Keep the 61.189 record of every test endorsement (name, kind of test, date, result) for at least 3 years.
cfi_notes: Three time windows meet at the instrument checkride. 61.65(d)(2)(i) counts the 3 airplane hours "within 2 calendar months before the date of the practical test" [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(i)]]; 61.39(a)(6)(i) and A.1 count training "within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application" [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)(i)]] [[12:40|AC 61-65K A.1]]; and A.44 says "within 2 calendar months preceding the date of the test" [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.44]]. Plan the last training so all three are clearly met.

AIH 9-13 says your 8710 signature and the logbook endorsement are valid for 60 days and should carry the same date [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]; the regulation uses calendar months [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)(i)]]. Teach the CFR wording and keep the two dates the same.

Devices for an IPC: 61.57(d)(2) lists an aircraft, FFS or FTD [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(2)]], while AC 61-98E 5.1.2 allows an AATD within its LOA [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.2]]. AIH 9-3 says ATDs cannot be used for airman practical tests [[25:173|AIH 9-3]], and an IPC is a check, not a practical test. Before planning an AATD IPC, read the device LOA and the current rule. AC 61-98E Appendix I also quotes an older wording of 61.57(d) ("flight simulator", "must consist of") [[15:46|AC 61-98E I-1]].

AIH C-4 says the instrument rating must be on the instructor certificate "as indicated in 14 CFR part 61, section 61.57(d)(2)" [[25:205|AIH C-4]], but 61.57(d)(2) is about where an IPC is given [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(2)]]. AC 61-98E bases the instructor requirement on 61.193 and 61.195 [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]]. Cite those.

A.71 says "in a [M/M] aircraft" [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.71]] although an IPC may be given in a FFS or FTD [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(2)]]. Application: when you use a device, name the device in the blank so the entry matches what happened.

AC 61-65K gives instrument applicants their own 61.39(a) endorsement, A.44, which already includes the knowledge test deficiencies [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.44]]; the general A.1 and A.2 cover the same 61.39(a)(6) items in two entries [[12:40|AC 61-65K A.1]]. The CFI lesson AI.II.K lists A.1 and A.2 next to the instrument endorsements; for an instrument test, A.43 plus A.44 is the AC set.

AC 61-98E 5.1.3.3 points to Appendix H for a sample IPC plan of action, while 5.4.2 points to Appendix I [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.3.3]] [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.2]]. Appendix H is a training and proficiency plan [[15:45|AC 61-98E H-1]]; Appendix I is the IPC checklist.

FAA-S-8081-9E's Area II note says the evaluator selects Tasks A and D, but its table for adding an instrument rating to a flight instructor certificate lists Area II Tasks A and C for an applicant who holds an airplane instructor rating, and its renewal table lists Task D and one other Task. Prepare Task D either way.

Application: have a study partner plant errors in a logbook copy (unsigned device time, a missing approach type, a stale knowledge test, a signature with no RE date) and find them out loud. It rehearses the K1 and K2 audit.
gaps: No source here gives sample wording for an ordinary instrument lesson entry; AC 61-65K Appendix A covers endorsements, and 61.51(h)(2) lists only what an entry must contain.

InFO 15012, Logging Instrument Approach Procedures, is named in AC 61-98E [[15:5|AC 61-98E 1.6]] but is not an uploaded source, so this lesson does not say when an approach in actual conditions may be logged or whether an instructor may count approaches the learner flies.

No source says whether the signature should show the instrument instructor rating (for example "CFII"); 61.51(h)(2)(ii) and AC 61-65K ask only for the certificate number and the RE or expiration date.
The Instrument Rating ACS (FAA-S-ACS-8) and its Rating Task Table for the IPC are not among the build sources.
No rule sets how long to keep an IPC plan of action ("an appropriate period") or device training records; the AIH suggests keeping training records at least 3 years [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

activities.title: Who logs it?
activities.intro: A rated private pilot flies the whole instrument lesson with you, partly in cloud and partly under the hood. Tap each item, then who logs it.

items.t: Simulated instrument time under the hood in VMC
Actual instrument time in cloud during the lesson
PIC time for the whole flight
Flight training received from an authorized instructor
The training endorsement with description, length, certificate number and RE date
Total flight time of the lesson

activities.why: Hood time is instrument time only for the pilot flying solely by instruments [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(1)]]; the instructor logs instrument time only in actual conditions [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(2)]]. The rated learner logs PIC as sole manipulator and you log PIC as the authorized instructor [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(e)(1)(i)]] [[60:229|14 CFR 61.51(e)(3)]]. You write the endorsement [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]]; each of you enters the date and total time in your own logbook [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(b)(1)]].

activities.title: Device time: what the entry needs
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then what the rules or the AIH call for.

pairs.l: FFS or FTD time toward the instrument rating
pairs.r: Instructor present to observe, who signs the record

pairs.l: ATD time used only for currency
pairs.r: A record of the device, the time and the content

pairs.l: Logging an FFS or FTD lesson
pairs.r: The FAA ID number or serial number of the device
BATD or AATD time, with manufacturer and model

pairs.l: Most BATD time creditable toward the rating
Most device time creditable outside part 142

activities.title: Count the hours and the months
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your learner logged 22 hours of instrument time in the airplane and 24 hours in an AATD, all with an instructor, not under part 142. How many hours count toward the 40?
items.why: AATD credit is capped at 20 hours, and so is all device time together outside part 142 [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(i)]] [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(j)]]: 22 + 20 = 42.

items.q: A learner has 12 BATD hours, 6 FTD hours (not part 142) and 25 airplane hours, all instrument time with an instructor. How many count toward the 40?
items.why: BATD credit is capped at 10 [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(i)]]; 10 + 6 = 16 device hours, under the 20-hour total cap [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(j)]]. 16 + 25 = 41.

items.q: A knowledge test was passed in March 2025. What is the last month of 2027 (as a number, January = 1) in which the practical test can be completed?
items.why: The test must fall within the 24 calendar months before the month the practical test is completed [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(1)]]. For March 2027 the window is March 2025 to February 2027, which includes March 2025; for April 2027 it does not.

items.q: In the last 24 calendar months you endorsed 7 applicants for practical tests and 6 passed the first time. What percentage passed the first time (nearest whole number)?
items.why: 6 / 7 = 0.857, about 86 percent. With at least 5 applicants and at least 80 percent passing, this meets one recent experience option [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(b)(2)(i)]].

items.q: You signed A.43 and A.44 for an applicant in May 2026. Until at least which year must your record of that endorsement be kept?
items.why: 61.189 records must be kept at least 3 years [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(c)]]: May 2026 + 3 years = May 2029.

activities.title: Which endorsement does what?
activities.intro: Drag each label to its pin on the AC 61-65K page.

pins.label: Knowledge test endorsement, after the 61.65(b) ground training
Practical test endorsement for the training of 61.65(c) and (d)
61.39(a) prerequisites for the instrument practical test
Certifies review of the areas missed on the knowledge test

activities.title: The IPC, step by step
activities.intro: Put the five steps of the AC 61-98E IPC checklist in order, then tap Check.
steps: Preparation: set expectations, regulatory review, assign a cross-country flight plan
Ground review: English language standard, preflight, departure, en route, arrival, approach and missed approach
Flight activities: aircraft control by instruments, systems and procedures, ADM, stabilized approaches
Postflight discussion: replay, reflect, reconstruct, redirect, and questions
Aeronautical health maintenance and improvement plan: personal minimums, practice plan, training plan
activities.why: Sequence from the sample IPC checklist [[15:46|AC 61-98E I-1]].

activities.title: True or false: the IPC
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: You may endorse an IPC that another instructor flew if you review her notes.
cards.why: False. You may endorse an IPC only if you tested the pilot under 61.57(d) [[60:347|14 CFR 61.195(d)(6)]].

cards.s: No logbook entry reflecting an unsatisfactory IPC is required.
cards.why: True [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.71]]. Log the session as dual instruction given [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.1]].

cards.s: An instructor giving an IPC in a single-engine airplane needs an instrument rating on both the pilot and the flight instructor certificate.
Sending an 8710-1 to the Airmen Certification Branch after an IPC is required.
cards.why: False. It is optional, though strongly encouraged [[15:8|AC 61-98E 1.10.2]].

cards.s: A BATD may be used for part of an IPC if its LOA allows it.
cards.why: False. Only AATDs may be used for the IPC [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.2]].

cards.s: The IPC must include the Instrument Rating ACS areas of operation for the rating held.

activities.title: Required record or good practice?
activities.intro: Tap each item, then whether 61.189 requires it.

items.t: Name, kind of test, date and result for each test endorsement you give
Name and date for each solo endorsement you give
Your signature in the logbook of each person you give ground training
Keeping those records for at least 3 years
The plan of action for each IPC
A training folder with lesson plans for each learner

activities.why: Required items are in [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189]]. The IPC plan of action is not required by 61.189 [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.2]]; the AIH recommends a training folder [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]; the 8710 for an IPC is optional [[15:8|AC 61-98E 1.10.2]].

activities.title: Sign or don't sign
activities.intro: You are a CFII at a busy school. Make each call as the day unfolds.

steps.s: 0800. A pilot asks you to sign 6 hours of AATD time he flew alone last month so it counts toward his instrument rating.
options: Sign it, since he shows you the device's printout of each session
Sign it as "reviewed," so it counts once an examiner checks it
Decline; it can count for currency if he records device, time and content
Sign it after he flies one more AATD lesson with you watching
steps.why: Device time counts toward a rating only if an authorized instructor was present to observe it and signs [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(4)]]. For currency, a record of device, time and content is enough [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(5)]].

steps.s: 1000. Your learner's checkride is in 10 days. Her last instrument training in the airplane was four months ago; since then she has flown only the AATD with you.
options: Endorse now; AATD time with you counts as recent training
Fly at least 3 hours of instrument training with her in the airplane first
Move the checkride into the AATD so airplane time is not needed
Endorse now and explain the gap to the examiner in a note
steps.why: 61.65(d)(2)(i) needs 3 hours of instrument flight training in an airplane within 2 calendar months before the test [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(i)]], and an ATD may not be used for the practical test [[12:9|AC 61-65K 12.4]].

steps.s: 1300. An IPC candidate flies to standard, but on the radio you doubt he meets the FAA English language standard.
options: Endorse the IPC; English is checked only on practical tests
Endorse the IPC and add an English limitation in the remarks
Give him a short written English test and endorse if he passes
Log the training, do not endorse completion, advise him, contact the FSDO
steps.why: If the pilot does not meet the AELS during an IPC, do not endorse it as complete; log the training received, advise the pilot and contact the responsible FSDO [[12:8|AC 61-65K 11.4.2]].

steps.s: 1500. Another IPC, in the school's C172, is satisfactory. The pilot hands you his logbook.
options: Write "IPC complete" and sign with your certificate number
Write A.71 with grade, certificate number, M/M, date and your full signature block
Write A.69, because an IPC also counts as his flight review
Write nothing; the 8710 you submit in IACRA is the record
steps.why: Use A.71 with every blank filled [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.71]] and the full signature block [[12:40|AC 61-65K A-7]]. An IPC from an instructor is not among the checks that replace a flight review [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(d)(1)]], and the 8710 is optional [[15:8|AC 61-98E 1.10.2]].

steps.s: 1700. Last week you signed A.43 and A.44 for a learner who passed today. What goes in your own records?
options: Her name, the kind of test, the date and the result, kept at least 3 years
Nothing; the examiner's file is the official record
A copy of her temporary certificate, and nothing else
Her total flight time and instrument time at the test
steps.why: Keep the name, kind of test, date and results for each person you endorsed for a practical test, for at least 3 years [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(b)]] [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(c)]].
